chapter: Harlem, Redman's band and the Savoy
title: Luis Russell's New Orleans band
summary: Russell's band filled in at Connie's Inn; Jackson lists its New Orleans players and praises Charlie Holmes's Hodges-like alto.

story.theme_name: Remembering the early trumpeters and their styles
story.community_name: Remembering King Oliver: the man, the band, the decline

blocks.x: Yeah. Well, you know, at one time Luis Russell used to have the house band there.
Oh, yeah. Did you know Luis Russell?
Oh, sure I knew Luis Russell. When I
first came to New York with Don, when Don would go out of town at Connie's Inn, Lou Russell would take the band in there.
Oh. What kind of guy was he?
Another guy that smiled. He was a kind of milquetoast, too, type of guy. He was --
A piano player, right?

Oh, yes. Oh, yes. He was from New Orleans. You know, that's the reason I think that Louie always, he always -- Louie always used him when he came to New York, you see, because they were all from New Orleans. Paul Barberin was in the band. He was Danny Barberin's cousin.
His uncle, I think, is --
Uncle or something, yeah, he was in the band then, Red Allen was in the band, Higginbotham was in the band.
This is Louie Russell's band?
That's right.
That was a good band. That was a New Orleans society.
It was in a way.
Yeah.
And Pop Foster was the bass player.
Right.
And Charlie Holmes was the first saxophone player.
Oh, yeah. I remember Charlie.

Charlie played closest to Johnny Hodges than any saxophone player I know. Duke even tried to get him once but Charlie wouldn't leave town. He was a real quiet type of guy and I think he never lived that down, too, about everybody saying he sounded like Johnny.
Uh-huh. Yeah, that could be a hangup.
It was. It was with him. And he was a little guy, like Johnny, too. He was about Johnny's height, you know.
That's beautiful.
Yeah.
